name: Waakye
summary: Rice and black-eyed peas cooked with dried millet leaves for a deep red-brown colour, served with shito and fried plantain.
story: Waakye is a beloved Ghanaian street food, especially at breakfast and lunch, sold wrapped in leaves with a generous array of sides. The rice and beans are traditionally coloured with dried sorghum leaf sheaths.

items.name: dried waakye (sorghum) leaves
items.note: or 1 tsp baking soda plus a little cocoa

steps.title: Start the beans
steps.text: Drain the soaked beans and put them in a large pot with the waakye leaves and 6 cups of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 35-40 minutes until the beans are just soft and the water is deep reddish brown.

steps.title: Remove the leaves
steps.text: Lift out the leaves and discard them. If you have no leaves, use the baking soda and cocoa substitute for colour. Leave the dark cooking liquid in the pot.

steps.title: Add the rice
steps.text: Stir in the rinsed rice and salt. The liquid should sit about 2 cm above the rice and beans; add boiling water if needed.

steps.title: Boil down
steps.text: Bring to a boil and cook uncovered for 8-10 minutes until the water has reduced to the level of the rice and little holes appear on the surface.

steps.title: Steam to finish
steps.text: Cover tightly and cook on lowest heat for 15-20 minutes until the rice is tender and each grain separate. Turn off the heat and rest for 10 minutes.

steps.title: Prepare sides
steps.text: While it rests, fry plantain slices in hot oil until golden and caramelised, peel the eggs and prepare the salad.

steps.title: Fluff and serve
steps.text: Fluff the rice gently with a fork; it should be deep brown-red. Serve with shito, eggs, gari, plantain, spaghetti and salad.

tips: Cook the beans separately first so they are tender when the rice is done.
Do not stir once the rice is covered or it turns mushy.
Shito is the heart of waakye, so serve generously.
Parboiled rice stays separate and firm.

swaps.swap: Look in African grocers; otherwise a pinch of baking soda with a teaspoon of cocoa gives colour but not the leaf's earthy flavour.
Cowpeas of any variety; red kidney beans work but the texture is heavier.
